title: "Letters criss-cross: rotate"

![Word Swirrel, level 2: the letters of the secret word scattered across the canvas, each one at a random position, in a random size, a random color, and tilted at a random angle.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstropek/ts-web-playground/main/exercises/0060-Arrays/word-swirrel-1.png){width=440}

In the first Word Swirrel, the scrambled word sat in the middle of
the canvas as one block of text. Level 2 makes it look the part.
Every letter gets its own place, its own size, its own color, and
its own tilt. Two ideas carry the whole chapter. First, a for loop
that visits a string one character at a time; you will write this
exact loop shape for the rest of the course. Second, a new
transformation: `rotate`, the missing sibling of `translate`, which
tilts everything you draw. Scrambling is not even needed anymore;
letters thrown all over the canvas are puzzle enough.

## AI tutor {#sec-tutor-criss-cross}

Rotation is famous for surprising beginners: you rotate a letter and
it swings to a completely different place. If that happens, tell the
tutor which transformation calls you make in which order, and where
the letter lands.

{{< tutor tutor-arrays >}}

## One letter at a time {#sec-letter-loop}

The scramble loop of the last chapter ate the word up. This chapter
needs something gentler: visit every character once, in order, and
draw it. That is a for loop over the indexes:

```typescript
for (let i = 0; i < wordToGuess.length; i++) {
    // wordToGuess[i] is the character of this round
}
```

Read the header with the indexes in mind: `i` starts at 0, the first
index. The loop runs while `i < wordToGuess.length`, and stops
exactly when `i` reaches the length, which is one past the last
index. For `"apple"` (length 5), `i` takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3,
and 4, every index once, none twice, no `undefined`. The `<` does the
off-by-one thinking for you; with `<=` the loop would run once too
often and read past the end.

Learn this loop by heart. "From 0, while less than length, one step
at a time" is *the* pattern for walking through anything that has
indexes, and the coming array chapters use it on every page.

## rotate: turning the paper {#sec-rotate}

You know `translate`; it moves the origin, and everything drawn
afterwards moves with it. `rotate` is its sibling: it turns the
whole coordinate system, and everything drawn afterwards is tilted.
The angle is in degrees, clockwise, as long as `angleMode(DEGREES)`
stands in `setup`, the same setting you used for `arc` in part 1.
Every program in this chapter sets it.

The catch: `rotate` turns the paper **around the current origin**,
the point (0, 0). A shape close to the origin tilts almost in place;
a shape far from the origin swings around it like a hammer thrower.
That is why rotation almost always comes as a team of three:

```typescript
translate(x, y);   // 1. move the origin to where the shape belongs
rotate(angle);     // 2. turn the paper around that point
text(letter, 0, 0); // 3. draw AT the origin
```

Move first, then turn, then draw at (0, 0). The letter sits at
(x, y) and is tilted by `angle`, and because it sits *on* the pivot
point, it tilts in place instead of swinging away. You met the same
draw-at-the-origin idea in the pattern recipe (@sec-cumulative);
rotation makes it essential.

::: {.callout-note}
## Rotate turns the system, not one shape
Like `translate`, `rotate` does not touch any shape that is already
drawn. It changes the coordinate system for everything that comes
after it, and a second `rotate` adds to the first. That is also why
the order matters: translate-then-rotate pins the letter to its
spot, rotate-then-translate makes the move itself happen in a tilted
direction.
:::

## The scatter recipe {#sec-scatter}

Now the loop and the transformation team up. One round of the loop
places one letter, and everything about the letter is random:

```typescript
for (let i = 0; i < wordToGuess.length; i++) {
    const x = random(MARGIN, WIDTH - MARGIN);
    const y = random(MARGIN, HEIGHT - MARGIN);
    const charSize = random(50, 150);
    const textColor = random(0, 360);
    const angle = random(-90, 90);

    push();
    translate(x, y);
    rotate(angle);
    fill(textColor, 100, 100);
    textSize(charSize);
    text(wordToGuess[i], 0, 0);
    pop();
}
```

A few details are worth a second look:

- **push and pop wrap every letter.** Translate and rotate calls add
  up, so without the note-taking, letter 2 would be measured from
  letter 1's tilted position, and the scatter would drift off the
  canvas. Each round starts fresh from the saved origin.
- **The random values are decimals.** So far you mostly wrapped
  `random` in `floor` to get whole numbers, like dice. Positions,
  sizes, and angles don't need whole numbers: `rotate(23.7)` is a
  perfectly fine tilt, so the `floor` stays away.
- **Negative angles are allowed.** `random(-90, 90)` tilts letters
  up to a quarter turn in either direction; a negative angle turns
  counterclockwise.
- **The color is HSB.** With `colorMode(HSB)` in `setup`,
  `fill(textColor, 100, 100)` with a hue from 0 to 360 gives full
  saturation and brightness, like in the colored rays.
- **MARGIN keeps letters visible.** The random position stays
  `MARGIN` pixels away from every edge, so even a big rotated letter
  is not cut off.

One more thing will greet you when you open level 2: the `guess`
function comes finished in the starter code. You built it yourself
last chapter; this time it is simply there, and your work happens in
`setup`.

## Your exercise: Word Swirrel (Level 2) {#sec-criss-cross-exercise}

1. **The loop without rotation.** Write the for loop with the
   random position, size, and color, but leave `rotate` out:
   translate, then draw the letter at (0, 0). Run it; the letters
   scatter, still standing upright.
2. **Add the tilt.** Put `rotate(angle)` between `translate` and
   `text`, run, and compare with the goal picture. If a letter
   seems to vanish, check the order of your three steps
   (@sec-rotate).
3. **Break it on purpose.** Comment out `push()` and `pop()` and
   predict the picture before you run. The transformations pile up,
   and the letters wander away. Put them back.
4. **Run it a few times.** Every run scatters differently, because
   `setup` runs once per start and asks `random` for fresh values
   each time. Play the game with a classmate: they guess, you
   check.
